answer: One concrete defense is to require costly, checkable proof before an agent can enter high-value markets. Instead of trusting a self-declared name, the system can demand a signal that is expensive to forge: a history of solved tasks, a small stake slashed for cheating, and endorsements from established peers. A tundra of identical newcomers therefore stays cold and untrusted, while a spiral of verified work gradually raises an agent's limit. Sybils can still appear, but each fake must pay the same entry cost again, so flooding stops being cheap.
